package.name: Entropy
package.description: Unpredictable bytes from the operating system

modules.name: Error
modules.header:
Why a request for unpredictable bytes did not produce them.
Four systems report the failure four ways — a negative error number, an `NTSTATUS`, and on Darwin no failure at
all — and a caller asking for a key does not want to know which. What a caller does want to know is whether to
try again, whether the source exists on this system, and whether the buffer holds anything.
One rule holds across every function in this package: a request either fills the whole buffer and succeeds, or
fails with one of these and leaves the buffer whatever it already held. There is no partial fill to inspect,
because a half-filled key is more dangerous than none at all — the first half looks exactly as random as a whole
one.

modules.name: Fill
modules.header:
The call a caller actually makes, and the seam that makes its failure paths testable.
`FillFromSource` is the system, reached directly. This is the layer above it: it splits a request larger than any
single call into as many calls as it takes, it zeroizes the whole buffer when any part of the request fails, and
it reaches the system through an interface rather than by name.
That last part is the point of the module. Entropy failures are the ones nobody tests: they need a kernel with no
generator, a process being signalled steadily, or a cryptographic provider that refuses — none of which a test
can arrange. So the source is an `EntropySource`, `SystemEntropy` is the one that asks the operating system, and a
test supplies one that fails exactly when the test wants it to. The code that handles a failure is then the same
code in the test and in production, which is the only way to know it works.

modules.name: Source
modules.header:
The system's own generator, reached the way each system wants to be asked.
Four systems, four interfaces. Linux and FreeBSD have a `getrandom` system call that may write fewer bytes than
asked for and may be interrupted by a signal, so a caller who needs the whole buffer has to loop — and looping
correctly is most of what this module is. Darwin's `arc4random_buf` is always seeded, never blocks and cannot
fail, so it returns nothing at all. Windows has `BCryptGenRandom`, which either fills the whole buffer or fails,
and reports through an `NTSTATUS` rather than an error number.
What comes out is fit for a key, a token, or anything an adversary would like to guess. It is not a generator:
there is no state here, nothing is reproducible, and drawing a lot of bytes at once is slower than drawing them
from a seeded generator. Ask for a seed here and take the rest from `Rux/Random`.
A failure leaves nothing usable behind. Whatever a short read managed to write is zeroized before the failure is
reported, because a half-filled key looks exactly as random as a whole one, and a caller who ignores a return
value should get an obviously wrong buffer rather than a subtly weak one.

doc.summary: Why unpredictable bytes could not be obtained.
doc.markdown:
Why unpredictable bytes could not be obtained.
Every case is a failure: nothing was written that a caller may rely on. A filled buffer is the success channel of
the `! EntropyError` the fill returns.

cases.name: Unsupported
cases.doc:
This system has no entropy source this package can reach.
A kernel too old for its own generator reports this. It does not change while a program runs, so retrying is
pointless.

cases.name: Interrupted
cases.doc:
The source kept being interrupted, and the call gave up rather than looping forever.
Ordinary on a process taking signals steadily. Worth one more attempt; not worth an unbounded number.

cases.name: Failed
cases.doc: The source refused for a reason the system did not make actionable.

cases.name: TooLarge
cases.doc:
The request was larger than the source accepts in one call.
Windows takes a 32-bit count, so a request above four gigabytes has no honest answer. Split it.

doc.markdown:
Whether trying again might work.
`self` is borrowed. True for `Interrupted`, which says a signal arrived rather than that anything is wrong.
False for everything else: a system with no source will not grow one, and a refusal repeated is still a
refusal.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

doc.summary: Something that can fill a buffer with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Something that can fill a buffer with unpredictable bytes.
Implemented by `SystemEntropy` for the operating system's generator, and by a test for a source that fails on
demand. An implementation either fills the whole buffer and succeeds, or fails with why it did not.

members.name: Fill
members.signature: func Fill(self: &var Self, buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. Succeeds only when every byte was written. An
implementation may write part of the buffer before failing — the caller is what guarantees nothing
partial survives.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written, or why not

doc.summary: The operating system's generator, as an `EntropySource`.
doc.markdown:
The operating system's generator, as an `EntropySource`.
Holds nothing: the system's generator needs no handle, no seed and no shutdown. It exists so that code taking a
source can be handed the real one.

The operating system's generator.
Takes nothing and cannot fail. Costs nothing to make, so there is no reason to keep one around rather than
making one where it is needed.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the source, which holds no state of its own

members.signature: pub func Fill(self: &var SystemEntropy, buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the operating system.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the operating system.
Exactly `FillFromSource`, reached through the interface. Succeeds only when every byte was written.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written, or why not

items.name: FillFrom
items.signature: pub func FillFrom(source: &var EntropySource, buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from `source`, in as many calls as it takes.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from `source`, in as many calls as it takes.
`source` is borrowed for the call; `buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. Succeeds only when
every byte was written, and otherwise fails with what the source reported.
A request larger than a single call accepts is split, so a caller need not know what that limit is. A failure
part-way through a split request is a failure of the whole request: there is no state in which some of a buffer
is unpredictable and the rest is not, because nothing downstream could act on the difference.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. On any failure the whole buffer is zeroized, including the parts an
earlier call filled successfully.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written, or why not

items.name: FillWithRetries
items.signature: pub func FillWithRetries(source: &var EntropySource, buffer: *var opaque, length: uint, attempts: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from `source`, trying again while the failure says trying again might work.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from `source`, trying again while the failure says trying again might work.
`source` is borrowed for the call; `buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` and `attempts` are read by value.
`attempts` is how many extra tries to make, so zero is one attempt and behaves exactly like `FillFrom`.
Only a transient failure is retried — `Interrupted`, which says a signal arrived rather than that anything is
wrong. A system with no source and a provider that refused are both reported at once, because repeating them
would only take longer to reach the same answer.
Runs in time proportional to `length` times the attempts made, and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. Every failed attempt zeroizes the buffer, so a failure that
exhausts the attempts leaves zeros.

params.name: attempts
params.markdown: how many times to go back to an interrupted source before giving up

doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written, or why not — `Interrupted` after `attempts` tries

items.name: Fill
items.signature: pub func Fill(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the operating system.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the operating system.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. This is the call to make when there is no reason to
name a source: it is `FillFrom` over `SystemEntropy`, with the same contract.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. On any failure the whole buffer is zeroized.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written, or why not

doc.summary: An unpredictable 64-bit value, which is what a generator wants for a seed.
doc.markdown:
An unpredictable 64-bit value, which is what a generator wants for a seed.
A failed draw scrubs its local copy before failing, so nothing of a partial draw is left behind on the stack.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: eight unpredictable bytes as a value, or why the draw failed

doc.summary: How many times a fill will go back to an interrupted source before giving up.
doc.markdown:
How many times a fill will go back to an interrupted source before giving up.
A signal arriving during the call is ordinary and retrying is correct, but a process taking signals steadily
must not spin forever inside what its caller believes is one operation. Reaching this reports `Interrupted`,
which says exactly that and leaves trying again to the caller, who knows whether it is worth it.

doc.summary: The largest request the source accepts in a single call.
doc.markdown:
The largest request the source accepts in a single call.
Windows takes a 32-bit count, so this is what a portable caller may ask for at once. A larger buffer is filled by
asking more than once, which `Fill` does.

items.name: FillFromSource
items.signature: pub func FillFromSource(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint) -> ! EntropyError

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the system's generator, in one pass.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` from the system's generator, in one pass.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. Succeeds only when every byte was written.
A zero length succeeds without touching anything. A length past what the source accepts is reported before the
buffer is looked at, so an impossible request is refused whatever was passed with it; a null buffer with an
ordinary length reports `Failed` rather than being written through.
On Linux and FreeBSD a short count is not a failure, so this loops until the buffer is full; a signal in the
middle is retried up to `MaxEntropyAttempts` times before reporting `Interrupted`. A kernel with no such call
reports `Unsupported`. On Darwin the source cannot fail. On Windows a request above `MaxEntropyRequest` reports
`TooLarge`, since the count is passed as 32 bits.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes. On any failure the buffer is zeroized, so a caller who ignores the
result gets zeros rather than a partly random buffer that would pass a glance.
doc.returns: nothing when every byte was written in this one pass, or why not
